title: Agile Is Dead, Long Live Agile
summary: When people say Agile is dead, they usually mean the ceremonies and the velocity charts. Here's how to tell which feedback loop broke, and a small way to repair each one.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
You've just come out of three meetings in a row. A standup where everyone read their ticket status to the Scrum Master. A planning session where the estimates got nudged, point by point, until they fit a date someone had already promised. A retro where the whole room knew the real problem and nobody said it out loud. Now you're in the pantry waiting for the kettle, and a teammate sighs: "Agile is dead." Nobody argues.

If that scene feels familiar, the sigh is fair. It's also not new. Dave Thomas, one of the people who wrote the Agile Manifesto in 2001, published a post called "Agile is Dead (Long Live Agility)" back in 2014. Some of the sharpest critics of Agile-the-industry are the people who started it. That's a useful hint about what actually died, and what's still worth keeping.

What people usually mean by "dead"

Plenty of developers never met Agile as a handful of values about feedback and working software. They met it as a calendar full of ceremonies, a Jira board that has to look tidy, a velocity chart that slowly turned into a performance score, and a vocabulary that makes common sense sound like a certification.

The people who were there at the start have said much the same. Thomas argued the word had become a marketing noun, sold by consultants and vendors, when it should have stayed an adjective describing how you work. In a 2018 talk, Martin Fowler called "the Agile Industrial Complex imposing methods upon people" an "absolute travesty", and described faux-agile as "agile that's just the name, but none of the practices and values in place" (The State of Agile Software in 2018). Ron Jeffries, another of the authors, wrote about story points: "I may have invented story points, and if I did, I'm sorry now." He added that comparing teams on velocity "is harmful" (Story Points Revisited).

So when someone says Agile is dead, they're usually describing a costume: Scrum performed for an audience, predictability that's mostly pretend, points treated as hours, retros with no power to change anything, and a culture that praises "responding to change" in the slide deck and punishes it in the roadmap review. That version deserves the criticism. Some of it deserves to go.

The part that never needed a brand

Underneath the costume is a loop that's older than any framework. Thomas boiled it down to four lines:

Agility in four lines

Find out where you are. Take a small step towards your goal. Adjust your understanding based on what you learned. Repeat.

The original principles say the same thing in other words. "Welcome changing requirements, even late in development." "Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project." "At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behavior accordingly." Even the Scrum Guide rests on three plain ideas: transparency, inspection and adaptation.

That loop is how a codebase gets better through review and refactoring. It's how a product gets less wrong after meeting real users. It's how a team notices a process is wearing people out and changes one habit before the damage becomes normal. We might stop calling it Agile one day. Just don't throw out the feedback loop with the label.

Easy to audit, hard to practice

Part of what went wrong is that Agile became easier to check from the outside than to practice from the inside. Anyone can see whether a team has a sprint planning, a daily, a review and a retro. The things that make those meetings worth having are much harder to see:

What an audit can see What actually decides whether it works
A daily standup happens every morning Someone can say "I'm stuck" and get help the same day
Every story has points Estimates start a conversation about risk and never get renegotiated to fit a date
Retros are on the calendar Last retro's action has an owner and actually happened
There's a Product Owner The PO shows up, and customer evidence can move the priority
The board is up to date The board is honest, including the work nobody wants to show

The left column is visible. The right column lives in how people treat each other. That's why a team can look less Agile on paper and still be the more agile one. Their planning is practical. Their daily is short because the board is already honest. Their retro produces one small change someone owns. Their estimates are conversations. When reality changes, they treat it as new information and leave the word "discipline" out of it.

The opposite happens too. A team can run every ceremony by the book and still be waterfall at heart. Requirements freeze early. Decisions only travel down. The team ships late because nobody wanted to be the one who raised the risk. Each sprint becomes a smaller box for the same old fear. Agile words can cover that for a while, and then people feel the gap between the words and the work. That's usually when the jokes start.

Ask what exactly died

So the next time someone says Agile is dead, skip the defense of the word. Ask which loop stopped working. Most complaints map to one of a few loops, and each one has a small repair you can try without a new framework:

What you hear The loop that broke One small repair
"Standup is a status report" The daily loop. The Scrum Guide says the daily exists "to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary" Walk the board right to left and ask what's blocking the goal. Skip the round of personal updates.
"Retros never change anything" The improvement loop Pick one action, give it an owner and put it in the next sprint backlog, which the Scrum Guide explicitly allows.
"Estimates are just pressure" The planning loop Stop comparing velocity across teams or people. Talk about the riskiest part of each story and leave the number for last.
"Feedback doesn't change the plan" The product loop Show something small to a real user this sprint, and agree up front on what result would change the priority.
"The process was handed to us" The team's say over its own work Let the team change one practice it finds useless. Fowler's line: "the team doing work decides how to do it."

If what died is ceremony without trust, good. If what died is estimation used as pressure, good. If what died is the idea that a framework can replace judgment, even better. If the habit of checking reality often and changing course with care died along with them, that's the one worth digging back up.

None of these repairs looks like a transformation. One clearer acceptance criterion. One smaller slice of work. One blocker raised a day earlier. One retro action that actually ships. Stack enough of them and you get a team that can change direction without breaking itself. If you want to see how the frameworks themselves fit in, there's how Scrum really runs day to day and Kanban vs. Scrum.

Try this week

  • Next time someone sighs "Agile is dead", ask them which meeting made them say it. Then find the loop in the table above.
  • Check last retro's action. If it has no owner, give it one before the next retro.
  • Run one standup around the sprint goal and the blocked items only, and see how long it takes.
  • Show one unfinished thing to a user or stakeholder before the sprint review.

faqs.a: The branded, ceremony-heavy version often deserves the criticism, and some of the sharpest critics are Agile Manifesto authors like Dave Thomas, Martin Fowler and Ron Jeffries. The habit underneath is still useful: find out where you are, take a small step, adjust based on what you learned, repeat. That loop doesn't need a brand to work.

faqs.q: Why do so many teams feel frustrated with Agile?
faqs.a: Many teams met Agile as process theater: standups that are status reports, story points treated as hours, velocity compared across teams, retros that never change anything, and a process handed down from above. Fowler calls the name-only version faux-agile. The frustration is usually with that implementation, and the original principles say almost the opposite.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Agile and agility?
faqs.a: Agile usually means the named frameworks, roles, ceremonies and vocabulary. Agility is the working habit underneath: get feedback early, keep the plan honest, slice work small enough to learn from, and change course when the evidence changes. Dave Thomas argued in 2014 that the word should describe how you work, and that agility is the part worth keeping.

faqs.q: How can a team get agility back without adding more process?
faqs.a: Ask which loop broke and fix that one. Run standup around the sprint goal and blocked work. Give each retro action an owner and put it in the next sprint backlog. Stop comparing velocity across teams. Show something small to a real user every sprint. Let the team drop or change one practice it finds useless.
